title: Perform and administer record keeping functions in poultry production

lessons.title: Why poultry farms keep records
lessons.html:
Records turn observations into decisions

A poultry house changes every day. Without records, a manager cannot tell whether a flock is doing well, find the cause of a problem, prove compliance or calculate profit. Records are also legal and commercial evidence: abattoirs, egg buyers, the vet, the state veterinary services and auditors may ask for them.

Types of records

RecordTypical content
PlacementDate, house, hatchery, breed, number of chicks, chick quality, hatchery vaccinations
Daily house sheetMortality, culls, feed, water, min and max temperatures, humidity, observations
WeightsWeekly sample weights, average, uniformity
Egg production (layers/breeders)Eggs collected, grades, floor eggs, cracked, egg weight
HealthVaccinations, treatments, vet visits, lab results, withdrawal periods
FeedDeliveries, ration type, quantity, silo levels
BiosecurityVisitor register, footbath changes, pest control
MaintenanceBreakdowns, services, generator tests
StaffAttendance, training, incidents
SalesBirds or eggs sold, weights, prices, abattoir results

Traceability

Records link each flock to its source, inputs, treatments and buyers. If there is a disease outbreak or a residue problem, traceability lets authorities and the company act quickly and limit damage.

Example

A broiler house shows water intake 8% lower than the day before. Because the worker recorded it, the supervisor checks and finds a blocked filter. It is cleaned before the birds lose weight. Without the record, the problem might not have been noticed until mortality rose.

Records also help with planning the next flock: placement numbers, feed orders and staffing can be based on real results rather than guesses.

Train every worker to understand why records matter.

lessons.title: Recording accurately
lessons.html:
Getting the data right

Principles

  • Timely: record at the time, or as soon as possible. Memory is unreliable.
  • Accurate: count dead birds, read meters exactly, use calibrated scales.
  • Complete: fill every field; write N/A if it does not apply.
  • Legible: neat handwriting in ink, or careful data entry.
  • Honest: never adjust figures to look better. Hidden problems grow.
  • Signed: the person who recorded and, where required, the supervisor who checked.

Correcting errors

On paper, draw a single line through the mistake, write the correct value and initial it. In electronic systems, use the edit function that keeps an audit trail; do not delete records.

Designing simple forms

A good daily house sheet has the farm, house and flock number at the top, one row per day, and clear columns with units, for example mortality (birds), feed (kg), water (litres), temperature (°C). Keep forms simple so that workers fill them in correctly. Place them where the work happens, such as in a clipboard at the house entrance.

Electronic and mobile systems

Many farms now capture data on phones or tablets, which sends figures straight to a central system and creates graphs. Make sure devices are charged, staff are trained, passwords are personal and data is backed up. Have paper back-ups for power or network failure.

Supervisor checks

Check records daily. Look for missing entries, impossible figures (such as water intake falling to zero) and unusual trends. Ask about them while the facts are fresh.

Keep blank forms stocked.

lessons.title: Analysing, filing and reporting
lessons.html:
Using records to manage

Calculations

  • Cumulative mortality % = total dead and culled ÷ birds placed × 100. Example: 900 ÷ 30 000 × 100 = 3%.
  • Feed conversion ratio = total feed used (kg) ÷ total live weight produced (kg).
  • Hen-day production % = eggs produced in a day ÷ hens alive that day × 100. Example: 8 550 eggs ÷ 9 500 hens × 100 = 90%.
  • Water to feed ratio = water used (litres) ÷ feed used (kg).

Graphs and trends

Plotting daily water intake, mortality or egg production on a graph makes changes easy to see. Compare actual figures with breed targets plotted on the same graph.

Filing and storage

  • File records by farm, house and flock so they can be found quickly.
  • Keep them in a dry, secure place, protected from pests.
  • Keep them for the period required by company policy, customers and authorities.
  • Protect personal information on staff records, as the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 requires.

Reporting

Prepare weekly reports for management with key figures, comparisons with targets, problems and actions. At the end of each flock, prepare a flock summary: placement, mortality, weights, FCR or egg production, health events, costs and lessons. Share the results with staff; it motivates them and shows why their recording matters.

Key points

  • Records support management decisions, compliance, traceability and audits.
  • Record at the time, accurately, completely, legibly and honestly.
  • Correct errors with a single line and initials, or with an audit trail electronically.
  • Calculate mortality %, FCR and hen-day production % and plot trends.
  • File records securely, protect personal information and report weekly and per flock.
